claim: A gain byte over a peaking section does not build the section at the gain it names. One section is stored at the top of the printed range and the byte blends it against the dry path, and a cut is that same section with its numerator and its denominator exchanged. The two readings agree at both ends of the window and at its centre and nowhere between, which is why nothing in this archive had noticed: at six decibels of a twelve decibel range the peak is about forty per cent narrower than the width byte asked for, and it is the width and not the height that says so -- every candidate here stands where the byte asked.
why_not_named: Whether the stored section is blended on the fly or a row per setting is held in ROM is not readable from outside the part: both give this curve at every setting. What is claimed is the curve and the two things about the part that produce it -- one stored section per entry rather than one per gain, and a cut that costs no second section.

document_rows.read_as: Evidence that a page prints a range of twelve decibels each way against those two addresses. What the claim takes from it is where the stored section sits, which is the top of that range -- not fitted here and not chosen, but the figure the gain class measured the window's ends at.

era_priors.claim: Building a filter section at an arbitrary gain is the expensive answer, and blending one stored section against the dry path is the cheap one.
era_priors.why: The coefficients of a peaking section want a sine and a square root of the gain, which a small control processor would rather not run on every parameter change; storing them instead costs a row per setting of the gain, on top of a row per entry of the tables beside it. Blending is neither: mixing a section's transfer towards unity leaves its denominator alone and makes its numerator three multiply-accumulates between two stored rows.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: The section at half its full gain had the width its width byte asks for, at a resolution the run can tell apart.

era_priors.claim: A cut costs no second stored section.
era_priors.why: The peaking section every filter cookbook of the period prints turns a boost into a cut by exchanging its numerator and its denominator, so a part that has the boost has the cut for nothing. A part that stored a second section at full cut and blended towards it instead would cut wider than it boosts, which is the asymmetry a constant-width graphic equaliser is known for.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: A cut of the same height as a boost came back a different width, which is what the second reading in this class predicts and what the cut side of these records was read for.

era_priors.claim: What is worth saving a stored row on is a section with tables behind it, not a shelf with two states.
era_priors.why: A mid section has sixteen centres and five widths behind it, so a row per gain setting would be eighty rows multiplied again. A shelf on this type has two corner states and no width, so there are two rows and nothing a blend would save.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: The shelves turned out to be blended too, which the one record that sweeps a shelf gain finely was read for.
era_priors.and_it_is_wrong: That is what happened. The shelves are blended, from the other end of the range -- inferences/roland-sc8850-01/section-gain-a-shelf-stores-the-cut.json. So this prior's cost argument does not hold: a part that has the blend does not stop using it where the saving is small. The claim above does not rest on it and never did -- the mid sections were measured, not inferred from an economy -- and it is kept here, marked, because a prior that turned out wrong is worth more to a reader than one quietly deleted. What is left of it is the part the shelf claim confirms: the number of stored rows does not decide which end the stored one sits at, because it costs the same either way.

adds: The records say what each setting of a gain byte did to the band profile. This claim is the step from that to how the byte reaches the section, which no record says and which the profile carries only in its width at the settings between the window's ends and its centre. What it adds over every model in this archive is that those models were wrong there: each of them builds its sections at the gain, and each of them was scored on records whose residual is smallest exactly where that is wrong.

alternatives.reading: The section is the cookbook section computed at the gain the byte names, or read out of a row stored per setting, which is the same curve.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: It says the feature is the width its width byte asked for at every setting of the gain, and the unit's is not: over 24 settings on two records it is out by 8.83 bands of a twelfth on average, always in the same direction, against the one band this reading resolves. Its residual over those records is three to five times the winner's.

alternatives.reading: The same blend, with the cut side blending towards a second section stored at full cut rather than inverting the boost.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: It is the winner on the boost side and cannot be told from it there. On the cut side it makes the feature wider as the cut shallows where the unit makes it narrower: 15 settings wrong and 11.42 bands out on average. It is also the only candidate here whose residual leans on a record. A cut that is the boost's mirror is what a coefficient swap gives and what this unit does.

alternatives.reading: The same blend with the one stored section at the bottom of the printed range rather than the top, so the near side of the byte is the cut and the boost is that inverted.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: It is this claim's winner turned over, it costs the same three multiply-accumulates, and it is the last of the four here: it makes the feature wider than the width byte asked for by about as much as building at the gain makes it wrong the other way -- 24 settings wrong and 16.45 bands out on average, the worst residual of the four, and the only reading here whose residual leans on two records. It is in the class because the shelves of this same type were measured to do it, which is why it was written and why the mid sections were put to it again.

alternatives.reading: The shelves are reached the same way, and what the shelf record shows is something about reading a shelf rather than about the path.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: Half of it was right and the half that decides was not. The count this class uses on a peak is the wrong instrument on a shelf -- it counts up from the bottom of the band set -- so what that count showed was indeed about the reading. Read a shelf's own way, on the same record and the same takes, the shelves are blended and they are not reached the same way: the stored section is at the other end of the range, which is the winner here turned over and the last of the four on these records. inferences/roland-sc8850-01/section-gain-a-shelf-stores-the-cut.json.

refuted_by: A peaking section at half its gain coming back the width its width byte asks for. Or a cut coming back a different width from the boost of the same height. Or a setting in the middle of the window whose profile is not the blend's, at more than the one band this reading resolves.

compared_against.generated_from: data/units/roland-sc8850-01/index.json, filtered to the efx-bands records of type 01 00 whose swept address is a mid gain byte, at the finest resolution published for each
compared_against.why_the_shelves_are_not_in_it: The two shelf gains carry this same byte and are left out by name. What tells these readings apart is the width of the feature, and a shelf has no width -- counting the bands it stands over half its height in counts the bottom of the band set. The shelf record was scored that way before the line was drawn and it refused the blend, which turned out to be the instrument and not the shelf: read a shelf's own way the shelves are blended too, from the other end of the range, and that is a claim of its own -- inferences/roland-sc8850-01/section-gain-a-shelf-stores-the-cut.json. Mixing the two into one score would have averaged two different answers into a third that is neither.

residual.unit: the median residual in decibels over the span the byte commands, meaned over the records that carry a feature
residual.why: Reported and not read. The settings that separate these readings are the ones whose profile is smallest, so they carry the least of a record's span and a residual meaned over it is nearly blind to them: the reading that is not blind is the width, and it is stated as a property. The residual still moves the right way -- three to five times better than the reading that builds at the gain on the records that ask -- and it is not what decided this.

gross.why: The median residual over the span the effect commands, taken as the worst of the records scored. A rejection bound and not a target: below it the residual is reported and never optimised, because no candidate is decided by it.

qualitative.why: Properties the unit's readings have that the model's readings must have too. No arithmetic over a residual rescues a model that cuts where the unit boosts.

power.beaten_by: leaning where the winner does not
power.why: The runner-up in the catalogue, scored on the same records, and whether it leans or contradicts a property where the winner does neither. The decoy is not chosen -- it is whichever candidate came second, so a strawman cannot be put up in its place. A class holding one candidate is a catalogue that is unfinished, which is a finding and not a pass.

breakdown.why: A point worse than 0.5 of the span is a failure at that point rather than error at it. A residual that leans with the setting or with frequency is pointing at a structure the model does not have; one that does not is pointing at the room and the converters, and is not made smaller by anything this project can do.

the_width_at_the_middle_of_the_window.what: How many bands of a twelfth the feature stands over half its own height in, at each setting four to nine steps from the centre of the window. Read off the unit's profile and off each rendering by one count, so whatever the band set does to a shape it does to all four.
the_width_at_the_middle_of_the_window.read_as: The unit's width moves with the gain, narrowing as the gain shrinks and doing it the same way on the boost and on the cut. The blend follows it band for band at every one of the 24 settings. Building at the gain gives one number for the whole window, which is the prediction the width byte's own claim rests on and which is right only at the ends. Blending towards a stored cut section follows the boost and runs the wrong way on the cut. Blending with the stored section at the cut end -- which is what the shelves of this same type do -- runs the wrong way on both.

what_the_shelf_did.what: The one record that sweeps a shelf gain at every setting between the window's ends. Scored the same way before this class was scoped, and then scored again a shelf's own way.
what_the_shelf_did.read_as: Under the peak's count it refuses the blend, and that is the count reading the bottom of the band set rather than the shelf. Under a reading of where the shelf falls away it is blended, with the stored section at the other end of the range: inferences/roland-sc8850-01/section-gain-a-shelf-stores-the-cut.json. What still scopes this claim to a peaking section is that the two answers are different, not that the shelf has none -- and the era reading that was offered for the difference, that a shelf has too few stored rows to be worth blending, is refuted by the same record.

what_this_does_not_close.what: What a shelf's gain does instead.
what_this_does_not_close.why: The blend looked refused, and what refused it was a peak's instrument used on a shelf.
what_this_does_not_close.what_would: A reading of a shelf's own shape applied to the record that is already on disk. No time with the unit.
what_this_does_not_close.what_it_turned_out_to_be: The shelf is blended as well, with the one stored section at the bottom of the printed range rather than the top -- the same three multiply-accumulates moved from the numerator to the denominator. The reading that answered is where the shelf has fallen to half of what it is at a band inside its own plateau, which is a position and not a width, because a shelf has no far side to have a width between.

what_this_does_not_close.what: The six other types that print a gain against a peaking section, and the combination types that print one against a mid section.
what_this_does_not_close.why: One type is read. The gain window itself was folded onto two combination types and holds there, but those runs asked the window's ends and four settings far outside it, which is the one part of the range where every reading in this class agrees.
what_this_does_not_close.what_would: Four settings in the middle of the window on one of them, which is four takes under a hold this archive has used twice.

what_this_does_not_close.what: Whether the stored section is blended at run time or held as a row per setting.
what_this_does_not_close.why: The two give the same curve at every setting the byte has, so no reading of this unit's output separates them. The difference is in ROM.

what_it_would_change: Every renderer of this line builds its equaliser sections at the gain asked for, because that is what a filter cookbook says to do. At the ends of the byte that is right and at every other setting it makes the peak too wide -- forty per cent at half gain, which is most of an octave on a mid section and is the part of a parametric equaliser a listener is setting the width byte for. It is also two lines of arithmetic to fix and it makes the gain cheaper rather than dearer.
a_note_on_how_it_was_nearly_missed: Three gates passed on the reading this refutes, on the same records, for two rounds. The residual is meaned over a record and the settings where the two readings differ are the ones whose profile is smallest, so they carry the least of the record's span; and the lean test looks for a residual that runs with the setting or with frequency, while this one is a hump -- nothing at both ends of the window and nothing at its centre. What found it was asking what the width was doing at the settings nobody had asked about, which is a reading and not a run.
